interviewees.org_description: Current employer is a pharma/biologics company (Abzena) operating under GxP/GMP regulation, described as small enough that his predecessor considered ServiceNow too complicated for end users. Prior employer, Thermo Fisher, described as a Fortune 500 company of roughly $40B revenue with about 2,000 sites, subject to SOC, ISO, GxP and SOC 2.
interviewees.tenure: About 6 months at Abzena at time of interview; prior tenure at Thermo Fisher not specified
interviewees.background: Serves as Senior Director of IT Infrastructure and Operations and describes himself as head of IT at his current company, overseeing infrastructure, applications, security and ITSM. His current company runs a custom ITSM platform that integrates with Microsoft Teams and uses AI to attempt troubleshooting before creating a ticket; that decision was made by his predecessor, who had previously had ServiceNow. At his previous employer, Thermo Fisher, he worked on a large ServiceNow environment covering Incident, Request, Problem, Change, Knowledge, full CMDB, Asset Management, Major Incident Management and HR, with GRC being implemented; the prior tool there was Zendesk. He described the vendor evaluation (Jira, BMC, Zendesk, Workday ticket management), the 9-12 month implementation, custom API integration work (Active Directory SSO, Workday, Databricks/legacy ERP), licensing surprises, and renewal price increases. At Abzena he says the removal of ServiceNow left an asset management gap and they are considering implementing the ServiceNow asset management piece for GMP equipment and IT assets.

expert-1.label: Scalability decided the选择
expert-1.statement: He returns to scalability as the criterion that mattered most: at ~2M tickets a year across a $40B, 2,000-site company, the prior tool would break, and ServiceNow's ability to scale outweighed its higher cost.

evidence.quote: I’d say scalability. We were at a point where the volume of data and manual workflows in our previous system wasn’t scalable. When we left it, we were at around 2M tickets per year, and trying to do that on the previous system would just break it. So scalability was the top criterion—working with a Fortune 500 company at roughly $40B revenue and 2,000 sites—this was critical.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: The business case focused on scalability. We were growing—from roughly a $20B company to about $30B—and adding around 10-50K users. We were already seeing performance issues, and ticket management wasn’t meeting GMP/GxP requirements.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: I think ServiceNow met the scalability challenges we were facing. We got the integrations we needed, as well as the automated workflows.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: GxP/SOX compliance shaped requirements
expert-1.statement: He repeatedly frames platform requirements in terms of regulated pharma operations: validated systems, GxP-flagged change workflows routed through Quality, and compliance as a criterion he would weigh above cost when considering a switch.

evidence.quote: Number one, the system was validated. For example, when you enter a change, you can check a box indicating it’s GxP-related. If it’s GxP-related, it triggers specific workflows for routing and the change process that Zendesk did not have.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: Yes, it was about consolidating a lot of the IT tools—some of it was even paper-based. We wanted to improve service levels and MTTR and also be able to track our assets. In addition, we wanted better compliance—we’re subject to heavy regulations such as SOC, ISO, GxP, and SOC 2.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: I would push back and question why that's the case. Cost might be one reason, but I would look at scalability, integration, and especially compliance from a regulatory perspective. We would look at things quite differently.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: Underestimated internal validation effort
expert-1.statement: The recurring cost and schedule surprise was internal labor, not licences: business-user testing and validation were underestimated, adding roughly 20-30% in soft cost and stretching a 6-7 month plan to 9-12 months.

evidence.quote: The biggest pain points were lacking a clear definition of done—there was so much customization that scope boundaries were fuzzy—and underestimating the internal effort required. User testing wasn’t clearly defined, so we had to pull in resources who weren’t expecting it, and it was hard to secure their time.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: In terms of expectations, the biggest miss was the internal level of effort and commitment—pulling additional resources for testing and validation. I’d say that added another 20-30% in cost. It’s soft cost, but we had to pull those resources away from other tasks.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: The implementation effort, and the common underestimation of the resources required for validation.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: Integration worked but was not plug-and-play
expert-1.statement: He rates integration as ServiceNow's strongest attribute and his top purchasing criterion, while stressing that in practice the integrations were built by hand — direct APIs, a middle layer for legacy systems — because out-of-the-box connectors did not reach their older data.

evidence.quote: I’d say the first is integration capabilities. At that scale, it has to work with your other systems. The second is scalability. Third would be cost, or total cost of ownership. Fourth, the user experience. And fifth, customization.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: It integrated well, but it took time to build. We set up single sign-on with Active Directory and integrated Workday. It wasn’t plug-and-play; our engineers and identity access management team had to do quite a bit of work.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: They had some out-of-the-box APIs, but we had legacy systems and tools that those APIs wouldn’t connect to, so we built a middle layer to make them talk. For example, we wanted to bring in Databricks data related to certain service tickets. There was a Databricks connector, but a lot of our legacy ERP data was feeding Databricks and the connector didn’t have access to it, so we wrote a custom API to integrate the two.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: Expensive and complex, especially for smaller firms
expert-1.statement: He consistently describes ServiceNow as roughly double competitors on cost and complex to configure and maintain — dedicated admins, licensing add-ons like GRC, approver roles — and says it can be overkill for smaller teams.

evidence.quote: As I mentioned before, ServiceNow’s implementation total cost of ownership was roughly double compared to its competitors.
evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: There were a few modules that ended up being additional costs we didn’t expect. For example, we thought GRC would be included, but it wasn’t. evidence.speaker: expert

evidence.quote: It's expensive, especially for smaller companies. There can be a steep learning curve. Implementations are complex and require more internal resources than expected. For smaller teams, it can be overkill.
evidence.speaker: expert

expert-1.label: AI posture is a differentiator

evidence.quote: At the time, they weren’t leaning into it as heavily; the vendor we chose was taking an AI-first approach. That was the major difference. Since then, I think they’ve grown in their AI capabilities. Cost was also a factor—we saw lower licensing costs.

evidence.quote: Obviously, cost is number one—many competitors are lower cost. But they typically don't have as much capability and flexibility as ServiceNow.
